sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A Dockerfile is a repeatable recipe for building an image. For a Go service it normally defines a build environment, downloads modules, compiles the command, and places the resulting binary plus required runtime files into a small final image.

Each instruction creates build state that Docker can cache. Copying `go.mod` and `go.sum` before source code lets dependency download stay cached when only application files change; a later `COPY` brings in the source for compilation.

For example, a builder based on the official Go image can run `go mod download` and `go build`, then a second stage copies `/out/server` into a minimal runtime image. The deployed image does not need the compiler or module cache.

A container shares the host kernel; it is not a virtual machine. A tiny `scratch` image only works when the binary and copied files are truly self-contained, including CA certificates, time-zone data, and any dynamic libraries the program uses.

Use a Dockerfile when the service needs a consistent, distributable runtime image for CI, testing, or deployment. Pin important base-image versions, keep the build context small, and make runtime configuration external to the image.

sections.title: The core model: a Dockerfile for a Go application
sections.content:
a Dockerfile for a Go application is easiest to understand by following the data or control from input to result. The details below form one connected model rather than a list of unrelated rules.

A useful Go image has two contracts. The build contract says which source, module graph, Go version, target operating system, and architecture produce the executable. The runtime contract says which user, files, certificates, ports, environment values, and signals the executable expects. Multi-stage builds let these contracts use different base images. Build caching works best when stable inputs appear before frequently changed source files. Image size matters, but correctness and patchability matter more than chasing the smallest possible number. Minimal images provide fewer tools for an attacker and fewer packages to update, yet they can also make diagnosis harder and omit files the service assumes exist. The final command should normally use exec form and run the Go process as PID 1 so termination reaches it. The service must then handle shutdown and stop accepting work before the container's grace period ends.

sections.title: a Dockerfile for a Go application example
sections.content:
~~~dockerfile
FROM golang:1.25 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN go mod download
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -trimpath -o /out/server ./cmd/server

FROM gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12:nonroot
COPY --from=build /out/server /server
USER nonroot:nonroot
ENTRYPOINT ["/server"]
~~~
